Keywords: House of Capet Fleur de Lis
RagShortTexts: The Capetian dynasty expanded the royal demesne under Louis IX's revered Christian justice.

Variants.Content: The Capetians had ruled France since Hugh Capet's election in 987, and the direct male line passed from father to son without a break until 1328. Under Louis IX the royal demesne grew, and the king's moral standing reached a new height. Royal bodies were laid in the abbey of Saint-Denis, and the golden fleurs-de-lis on azure became the emblem of French kingship. Louis centralized justice through itinerant royal inspectors, the enquêteurs, who heard complaints against local officials, and through the Parlement of Paris, which grew into the kingdom's highest court. His reforms made the crown the most respected judge in Christendom.

Cadet branches of the family, most notably the house of Anjou, carried Capetian ambitions into southern Italy and the crusader principalities. Charles of Anjou seized the kingdom of Sicily in 1266, which tied the French crown to papal wars against the Hohenstaufen. Royal envoys from Paris were courted by rival princes, so the Capetian court became the place where disputes were arbitrated.
Commoners revere King Louis dispensing open-air justice beneath the Oak of Vincennes, where any aggrieved pauper can petition the crown without aristocratic intimidation.
